messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 38
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Community Organizer
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 62

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Entrapment: Having no options, Intrusive Memory: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly, Discomfort: Feeling uncomfortable
  Maladaptive Strategies: Sit With Back to Wall: always sit with back against a wall to see the room, Memory Erasure: I try to erase the memory of the event, Overworking: I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied
  Threat: Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
  Memory: Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank, Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
  Negative Appraisals: Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside, Others-Would-Cope: Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening, Weakness Belief: I am a weak person

Vignette:
Marisol Alvarez is a 38-year-old community organizer who came to treatment after years of arranging her life around a sense of danger she could not easily explain to other people. She grew up in a home where physical abuse by a caregiver was an ordinary possibility, and one childhood incident stands out in the way she remembers it now: not as a smooth story, but as a set of images. She can describe the sharp visual fragments with striking precision—the caregiver closing off the doorway, the look of the room from her height, the sense of having nowhere to go—while large stretches around those moments are simply absent. What remains most potent is the feeling of entrapment. In her memory there were no options, no way past the adult blocking her, no one coming, no move she could make that would change what was about to happen. Sometimes she recounts those moments in a flat, detached way that startles even her, as if she is talking about something that happened to another girl. At other times the images arrive suddenly and without warning, vivid enough to interrupt whatever she is doing.

As she got older, Marisol did not think of herself as someone who had been injured so much as someone who had failed at something essential. She had come to believe that a stronger person, a quicker person, somebody else, would have stopped it. The conclusion she carried into adult life was brutally simple: she was weak. That belief sat beside another feeling she found harder to name, a deadness inside that appeared at odd times and made her feel cut off even from experiences that should have mattered to her.

In adulthood, these patterns became woven into the way she moves through the world. Her work as a community organizer keeps her in church basements, school cafeterias, neighborhood association meetings, and tense public forums where people pack tightly into rows of folding chairs. Before she can pay attention to the agenda, she scans the room and chooses her seat according to how protected it feels. She always sits with her back against a wall if she can, preferring a clear view of the door and everyone entering. If someone has taken the seat she wants, she becomes sharply uncomfortable, distracted by the sense of exposure until she can reposition herself. In crowded meetings, especially when people cluster around exits or she feels hemmed in by bodies and noise, the old sensation of having no options can flash up so quickly that an image from childhood cuts across the present. She may not even have words for it in the moment; it is just a jolt of discomfort and a sudden need to orient herself.

Outside work, Marisol often checks behind her when walking to her car, on sidewalks after evening events, or even in broad daylight between appointments. She knows this can look excessive, yet she feels unable to settle unless she has confirmed who is around her. Night is its own struggle. Falling asleep feels like giving up vigilance, and she lies awake listening, alert to the apartment and the street beyond it, as if staying watchful is necessary. Her partner has noticed that she startles at small sounds and stays awake long after saying she is tired, but Marisol tends to minimize it or go quiet.

For years she has tried to deal with the memories by pushing them away. When an image intrudes, she attempts to erase it, mentally swatting it aside before it can develop into anything more. More reliably, she throws herself into work. She takes on extra planning, more calls, more outreach, more tasks than her role requires, keeping her schedule crowded enough that there is little room for stillness. Colleagues value her dedication, but the cost has become visible. She stays late, has trouble stepping back, and arrives at meetings already tense. At home, her partner experiences her as physically present but hard to reach, especially during periods when Marisol says she feels nothing at all.

She sought help after a recent stretch of back-to-back organizing meetings left her exhausted and increasingly unsettled. During one crowded gathering, she found herself unable to focus on the speakers because she was preoccupied with where she was sitting, who was behind her, and how quickly she could leave if she needed to. Later that night she could not sleep, and a visual fragment from childhood came to mind so abruptly that she sat up in bed feeling both numb and deeply shaken. What finally brought her in was not only the fatigue, but the fear that this constricted way of living had become normal for her. She wants to know whether she can feel less guarded and less dead inside. What frightens her most is the possibility that the weakness she has always believed in herself is simply who she is.
